My new book, Co-Existence, is out today.  It is a guide to how to live & work in a world where AI is sometimes, but not always, better than you.

(And, for the release, I worked with Opus 5.5 to make a quite interesting experience for the book's website:

The counterexample to AI diffusion taking a long time is coding, where the complete transformation of a profession is well underway less than a year after real working coding agents. Faster than I would’ve expected given historical technological adoption rates in professions.
Hey, remember “talk to your documents” RAG-based solutions as the future of AI? Crazy times a year and a half ago.

Anyhow, in a little over a week we will see the release of The Last Human Game.

There will never be another AAA game at the scale of GTA 6 with no AI assistance. People will look back at an all-human game with a billion dollar budget and wonder how they did it, like the Pyramids
One of the most significant things about Gemini 4 Carbon is that it is showing that Google is back in the race of frontier models, rapid releases and rapid improvement.

Looks like Fable 5.2 is above the already steep trendline on three of the most informative unsaturated benchmarks (ECI is a composite of other benchmarks, Remote Labor measures the ability to do end-to-end freelance jobs, RoboDojo involves controlling robotics).

In addition to more serious examples I shared in my post, I had Fable 5.2 build a parody reverse Scooby Doo game where you have to scare away meddling kids. Here is the trailer it made (including the music and sounds) and the game (which is fun) is here:

I had early access to Fable 5.2 for a bit & I think  it crosses the line into being a sort of Jagged AGI. Here, I have it launch a business, do academic research, hack hardware, build 3D models & more. I think it is a good illustration of limits & powers:

A favorite optimistic view of the future of AI is from a pessimistic book that not about AI: "Rise and Fall of American Growth," which argues that we had a one-time explosion in living standards from 1870 and 1920 (& later outside the US).

In 1870: no toilets, no city plumbing, lamp light, no central heating, little public health, horses for local travel, etc. In 50 years, all of this was solved & the nation was electrified. In the next fifty modern medicine, air travel and telecommunication happened.

The book then points out that we have had no changes in lifestyle of similar scale since the 1970s. Written in 2016, it argued that we would likely never experience another boom like the "Special Century." The positive view of AI should make us ask "But what if we do?" and "How do we make it all go right?"

It isn't that weird to think that "this time is different" - we had a couple of Industrial Revolutions over the past couple centuries, just because we got used to a relatively steady-state regime post World War Two with a regular pace of growth doesn't mean it continues forever.
